stem: A surface receives 750 W of solar radiation and scatters 180 W back into space. What is its albedo?
explanation: Albedo = scattered power / incident power = 180/750 = 0.24.
sourceNote: Original IB Physics B.2 question. Benchmarked against user-provided Paper 1A samples and B.2 syllabus.

stem: Two equal-area surfaces receive the same solar intensity. Surface X has albedo 0.15 and surface Y has albedo 0.65. What is the ratio of power absorbed by X to power absorbed by Y?
explanation: Absorbed fractions are 0.85 and 0.35. Their ratio is 0.85/0.35 = 2.43 ≈ 2.4.
sourceNote: Original IB Physics B.2 question. Benchmarked against user-provided Paper 1A samples and B.2 syllabus.

stem: A planet radiates as a black body. Its absolute surface temperature rises by 10%, while its radius stays constant. What is the approximate percentage increase in its emitted power?
explanation: P ∝ T⁴ for fixed area. (1.10)⁴ = 1.4641, so the emitted power increases by approximately 46%.
sourceNote: Original IB Physics B.2 question. Benchmarked against user-provided Paper 1A samples and B.2 syllabus.

stem: At a particular temperature, a black surface emits 960 W m⁻². A real surface at the same temperature emits 624 W m⁻². What is the emissivity of the real surface?
explanation: Emissivity = 624/960 = 0.65. It is dimensionless and cannot exceed 1 in this model.
sourceNote: Original IB Physics B.2 question. Benchmarked against user-provided Paper 1A samples and B.2 syllabus.

stem: Which gas is a significant greenhouse gas because its molecules can absorb selected frequencies of terrestrial infrared radiation?
explanation: Methane has infrared-active molecular vibrations. The main atmospheric constituents N₂, O₂ and Ar do not absorb terrestrial infrared strongly by the same mechanism.
sourceNote: Original IB Physics B.2 question. Benchmarked against user-provided Paper 1A samples and B.2 syllabus.

stem: The solar constant at the orbit of a planet is S. The planet is spherical and receives parallel solar rays. What is the average incident solar intensity per unit area of its entire surface?
explanation: The planet intercepts SπR² and has surface area 4πR², so the global mean is S/4.
sourceNote: Original IB Physics B.2 question. Benchmarked against user-provided Paper 1A samples and B.2 syllabus.

stem: A star has constant luminosity. Planet B orbits at three times the distance of planet A. What is the ratio of the solar constant at B to that at A?
explanation: I = L/(4πr²). Increasing distance by a factor of 3 reduces intensity by a factor of 9.
sourceNote: Original IB Physics B.2 question. Benchmarked against user-provided Paper 1A samples and B.2 syllabus.

stem: A planet has solar constant 1200 W m⁻² and albedo 0.20. What is its mean absorbed solar intensity over its whole surface?
explanation: Mean incident intensity = S/4 = 300 W m⁻². Absorbed fraction = 0.80, giving 240 W m⁻².
sourceNote: Original IB Physics B.2 question. Benchmarked against user-provided Paper 1A samples and B.2 syllabus.

stem: Two otherwise identical, airless planets orbit the same star at the same distance. Planet X has albedo 0.36 and planet Y has albedo 0.59. Both are black-body emitters. What is the ratio of equilibrium temperature of X to that of Y?
sourceNote: Original IB Physics B.2 question. Benchmarked against user-provided Paper 1A samples and B.2 syllabus.

stem: A black-body surface at 300 K emits an intensity I. At what temperature will it emit an intensity 16I?
sourceNote: Original IB Physics B.2 question. Benchmarked against user-provided Paper 1A samples and B.2 syllabus.

stem: An airless planet has constant albedo and solar input. Its thermal emissivity falls from 0.81 to 0.16. If it remains in radiative equilibrium, by what factor does its equilibrium temperature change?
explanation: At equilibrium εσT⁴ equals fixed absorbed intensity. Tnew/Told=(0.81/0.16)^(1/4)=1.50.
sourceNote: Original IB Physics B.2 question. Benchmarked against user-provided Paper 1A samples and B.2 syllabus.

stem: A simplified surface energy budget is shown. What is the net rate of energy gain per square metre of the surface?
explanation: Incoming = 210 + 100 = 310 W m⁻². Outgoing = 250 + 30 = 280 W m⁻². Net gain = 30 W m⁻².
diagramAlt: Surface energy budget: incoming solar 210, incoming atmospheric infrared 100, emitted infrared 250, and convection 30, all in W per square metre.
sourceNote: Original IB Physics B.2 question. Benchmarked against user-provided Paper 1A samples and B.2 syllabus.

stem: A greenhouse-gas molecule absorbs infrared radiation emitted by Earth. Which description best explains the warming effect in a simple atmospheric model?
options: The molecule permanently stores all the absorbed energy.
The molecule changes the infrared radiation into visible light only.
The energy is re-emitted in various directions, including towards the surface.
The molecule reflects incoming sunlight directly back to the surface.
explanation: Infrared-active molecules absorb and exchange energy through molecular modes, and atmospheric thermal radiation is emitted in all directions. Part of the downward radiation reaches the surface.
sourceNote: Original IB Physics B.2 question. Benchmarked against user-provided Paper 1A samples and B.2 syllabus.

stem: Why can carbon dioxide absorb some infrared wavelengths but not all wavelengths equally strongly?
options: Its allowed molecular energy changes correspond to particular photon energies.
Its molecules travel at only one speed.
It absorbs every wavelength shorter than visible light.
Its absorption is controlled only by the total number of atoms.
explanation: Molecular rotational-vibrational transitions have quantized energies, so absorption depends on photon frequency and transition selection rules.
sourceNote: Original IB Physics B.2 question. Benchmarked against user-provided Paper 1A samples and B.2 syllabus.

stem: Which process most directly contributes to the enhanced greenhouse effect over the long term?
options: More infrared radiation passing freely through the atmosphere.
Combustion of fossil fuels increasing atmospheric CO₂.
A decrease in the number of infrared-active molecules.
A permanent reduction in Earth’s solar constant.
explanation: Burning fossil fuels adds CO₂ to the atmosphere, increasing the absorption and emission of terrestrial infrared radiation.
sourceNote: Original IB Physics B.2 question. Benchmarked against user-provided Paper 1A samples and B.2 syllabus.

stem: In a simplified steady-state one-layer atmosphere, the atmosphere absorbs all terrestrial infrared radiation, is transparent to sunlight, and radiates equally upward and downward. If the outgoing infrared intensity to space is 240 W m⁻², what is the infrared intensity emitted by Earth’s surface?
explanation: The atmosphere emits 240 W m⁻² upward and 240 downward, so it emits 480 in total. Steady-state atmosphere absorbs 480 W m⁻² from the surface, so the surface emits 480 W m⁻².
sourceNote: Original IB Physics B.2 question. Benchmarked against user-provided Paper 1A samples and B.2 syllabus.

stem: A region receives solar radiation at 680 W m⁻². Its albedo increases from 0.25 to 0.40 while the incoming intensity stays fixed. By how much does the absorbed intensity change?
explanation: Absorbed intensity changes from 0.75×680=510 to 0.60×680=408 W m⁻², a decrease of 102 W m⁻².
sourceNote: Original IB Physics B.2 question. Benchmarked against user-provided Paper 1A samples and B.2 syllabus.

stem: Two spherical planets have the same temperature and emissivity. Planet Q has 1.5 times the radius of planet P. What is the ratio of total thermal power emitted by Q to that emitted by P?
explanation: P=εσ(4πR²)T⁴, so emitted power scales with R². Ratio=1.5²=2.25.
sourceNote: Original IB Physics B.2 question. Benchmarked against user-provided Paper 1A samples and B.2 syllabus.

stem: The stellar luminosity doubles and the orbital radius of a planet increases by a factor of √2. What happens to the solar constant at that planet?
explanation: S=L/(4πr²). Both luminosity and r² double, giving no net change.
sourceNote: Original IB Physics B.2 question. Benchmarked against user-provided Paper 1A samples and B.2 syllabus.

stem: A planet receives a mean incident solar intensity of 320 W m⁻² and reflects 25% of this radiation. It emits infrared radiation with emissivity 0.80. At equilibrium, what black-body emitted intensity σT⁴ corresponds to its surface temperature in the simplified airless model?
explanation: Absorbed intensity=(1−0.25)×320=240 W m⁻². At balance εσT⁴=240; hence σT⁴=240/0.80=300 W m⁻².
sourceNote: Original IB Physics B.2 question. Benchmarked against user-provided Paper 1A samples and B.2 syllabus.

stem: Which change would most directly cause Earth’s average albedo to increase, assuming other conditions unchanged?
options: An increase in the area covered by fresh snow.
The melting of bright sea ice into darker ocean water.
A reduction in low-level reflective clouds.
An increase in absorption by dark land surfaces.
explanation: Fresh snow typically reflects a larger fraction of incident shortwave radiation than the darker surfaces it replaces.
sourceNote: Original IB Physics B.2 question. Benchmarked against user-provided Paper 1A samples and B.2 syllabus.

stem: Surface X has temperature 400 K and emissivity 0.50. Surface Y has temperature 300 K and emissivity 1.0. What is the ratio of emitted thermal intensity from X to that from Y?

stem: Which pair of human activities directly increases the atmospheric concentration of two different greenhouse gases?
options: Cattle farming and heavy use of nitrogen fertilizers.
Reforestation and reduction of fossil-fuel combustion.
explanation: Cattle digestion can release methane (CH₄), and nitrogen fertilizer use can lead to nitrous oxide (N₂O) emissions.
sourceNote: Original IB Physics B.2 question. Benchmarked against user-provided Paper 1A samples and B.2 syllabus.

stem: An airless planet has albedo 0.19 and equilibrium temperature 270 K. Its solar constant changes but its albedo and emissivity remain unchanged. What solar-constant factor would increase its equilibrium temperature to 300 K?
explanation: S∝T⁴ when albedo and emissivity stay constant. Ratio=(300/270)⁴≈1.52.
sourceNote: Original IB Physics B.2 question. Benchmarked against user-provided Paper 1A samples and B.2 syllabus.

stem: A simplified model predicts that a planet’s equilibrium temperature rises when more of its outgoing infrared radiation is absorbed by its atmosphere. Which statement identifies an important limitation of this model?
options: It assumes all radiation travels through a vacuum.
It neglects effects such as convection, clouds and wavelength-dependent absorption.
It assumes solar radiation travels toward the planet.
explanation: Simple radiative models omit important processes such as convection, spatially variable clouds and spectrally selective absorption and emission.
sourceNote: Original IB Physics B.2 question. Benchmarked against user-provided Paper 1A samples and B.2 syllabus.
